title: Look at the eye
context: A person in a famine-affected area with night blindness and dry eyes.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC
img.alt: Close view of a left eye with a keratinised, foamy-looking plaque on the conjunctiva.

hints: The patch looks foamy, like dried soap.
The night blindness points to a fat-soluble vitamin.
why: A foamy, keratinised plaque on a dry conjunctiva.
pearl: Vitamin A deficiency is a leading cause of preventable blindness in children worldwide. Severe measles can tip a child into it, which is why vitamin A is part of measles treatment.

title: Itchy spots, all over
context: A 24-year-old childcare worker with a mild fever and an itchy rash that started on her trunk two days ago.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/K.L. Herrmann
img.alt: Close-up of skin with clear fluid-filled blisters on red bases and one crusted lesion.

hints: Look closely: some spots are fresh blisters, others are already crusting.
Classically described as 'dewdrops on a rose petal'.
why: Clear vesicles on red bases alongside crusted lesions: crops at different stages at the same time, the hallmark of varicella.
pearl: Lesions at different stages side by side means chickenpox; all at the same stage should make you think of smallpox or mpox. Adults and pregnant women get sicker, so antivirals matter more.

title: A painful stripe
context: A 68-year-old with three days of burning pain on one side of the trunk, now with a rash in the same spot.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/K.L. Herrmann
img.alt: A band of clustered red papules and vesicles on the trunk following a single dermatome (T10–T11).

hints: It stops sharply at the midline.
The pain came before the rash.
why: Clustered vesicles on red skin in a band following a single dermatome, on one side only.
pearl: Start antivirals within 72 hours of rash onset. Vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) mean the eye may be involved. A vaccine is available for older adults.

title: Tender shins
context: A 27-year-old woman with painful red lumps on both shins, achy joints and a recent sore throat.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: Dr. R. Huntington
img.alt: Front of both shins with raised, red, tender-looking nodules.

hints: The lumps are deep in the fat under the skin.
They heal like a bruise, without scarring.
why: Tender, raised red nodules over both shins: inflammation of the fat beneath the skin (panniculitis).
assoc: Pregnancy and the oral contraceptive pill
pearl: Erythema nodosum with hilar lymphadenopathy is Löfgren's syndrome (sarcoidosis), which usually settles by itself. Check for strep, TB, IBD and medicines.

title: Look at the legs
context: A child with poor growth and little sunlight, who was slow to walk.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC
img.alt: A malnourished child's legs with bowed knees (genu varum).

hints: The problem is with mineralising growing bone.
Sunshine and diet both matter here.
why: Bowed legs (genu varum) from soft, poorly mineralised growing bones.
pearl: Some bowing is normal in toddlers, but progressive or one-sided bowing needs a look. Rickets is making a comeback in children with dark skin, covering clothing or little sun.

title: A black scab
context: A farm worker who skinned a sick cow last week. The sore isn't painful, but the arm is swollen.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Archil Navdarashvili, Georgia (Republic) (cropped)
img.alt: A man's forearm with a large lesion covered by a dark brown-to-black scab.

hints: The black scab is called an eschar, and it's painless.
The bacterium forms spores that survive in soil for decades.
why: A large black eschar on the forearm with surrounding swelling.
pearl: A painless black eschar with a lot of swelling around it should prompt you to ask about animals and hides. Cutaneous anthrax is very treatable with antibiotics, but notify public health.

title: Look at the palms
context: A 31-year-old with a sore throat, patchy hair loss and a non-itchy rash, a couple of months after a painless sore that healed.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC
img.alt: Close-up of both palms with a scaly, darkened papular rash.

hints: The rash is on the palms and soles, which narrows the list fast.
Think of the 'great imitator'.
why: Scaly, coppery-brown papules on both palms.
pearl: Rashes on the palms and soles have a short list: secondary syphilis, hand, foot and mouth disease, erythema multiforme and some rickettsial infections. Syphilis rates are rising, including congenital syphilis.

title: A historical image
context: This photo was taken before 1980. The patient had high fever and back pain, then a rash that began on the face and arms.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC
img.alt: A knee and thigh covered in raised fluid-filled lesions, all at the same stage.

hints: Every lesion is at the same stage.
Declared eradicated in 1980.
why: Dense, firm, deep-seated lesions over the knee and thigh, all at the same stage.
assoc: Centrifugal rash (face and limbs more than trunk)
pearl: Smallpox lesions are all at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs; chickenpox is mixed-stage and mostly on the trunk. Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated so far.

title: A spreading ring
context: A hiker in the northeastern US with fatigue and a slowly expanding, painless red patch on the arm, a week after a weekend camping.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC/James Gathany
img.alt: A bull's-eye shaped red rash at a tick-bite site on the back of an upper arm.

hints: It grew bigger, day by day, from one spot.
Something small and eight-legged may have bitten here.
why: A large bull's-eye red patch that expanded outward from a tick-bite site.
pearl: Erythema migrans is diagnostic of early Lyme disease in an endemic area, so treat without waiting for serology, which is often negative this early. Lyme disease acquired locally in Australia has not been proven.

title: Something white
context: A 72-year-old using an inhaled steroid for COPD, with a sore mouth and an odd taste.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Sol Silverman, Jr., DDS
img.alt: Close intraoral view with creamy white plaques on the oral mucosa.

hints: The white patches wipe off, leaving red, raw spots.
Rinsing after the puffer helps prevent it.
why: Creamy white plaques on red oral mucosa that can be scraped away.
pearl: Thrush wipes off; leukoplakia and oral hairy leukoplakia don't. Unexplained thrush in a young adult deserves an HIV test.

title: Press and look
context: A woman in a community where the staple food is polished white rice, with weakness and swollen legs.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC (cropped)
img.alt: A health worker pressing a thumb into a woman's shin, leaving a dent of pitting oedema (beriberi).

hints: The examiner is pressing a thumb into the shin.
Here the cause is a vitamin B1 deficiency (wet beriberi).
why: A thumb pressed into the swollen shin leaves a dent: fluid in the tissues that can be pushed aside.
pearl: Pitting oedema means excess tissue fluid. Lymphoedema and myxoedema are usually non-pitting. Diets based on polished rice can cause thiamine deficiency.

title: Look at the fingertips
context: A person with a long-standing lung problem and chronic cough. Check the hand.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Behrens
img.alt: Back of a child's left hand showing clubbed fingertips.

hints: Try Schamroth's window test.
The nail-bed angle is lost.
why: Bulbous fingertips with loss of the normal angle between the nail and nail fold.
pearl: Clubbing is not a feature of uncomplicated COPD, so new clubbing in a smoker needs a chest X-ray to look for lung cancer.

title: Look at the throat
context: An unvaccinated traveller with a sore throat, low fever and a very swollen neck.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Carl Flint
img.alt: View into the throat showing an adherent grey membrane over the right tonsil and nearby pharynx.

hints: The grey coating bleeds if you try to scrape it off.
The neck swelling is sometimes called a 'bull neck'.
why: A thick grey membrane stuck over the tonsil and spreading onto the throat.
assoc: Myocarditis and nerve damage from the toxin
pearl: The pseudomembrane bleeds when scraped, unlike tonsillar exudate. Give antitoxin early, as well as antibiotics, and notify public health. Vaccination has made it rare, but outbreaks happen.

title: Side of the tongue
context: A 38-year-old's dentist noticed these painless patches at a routine check-up.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Sol Silverman, Jr., DDS
img.alt: Close intraoral view of white corrugated patches on the side of the tongue.

hints: Look at where it sits and its texture: vertical ridges on the side of the tongue.
The cause is the same virus behind glandular fever, and it only gets away with this when immunity is down.
why: White, corrugated patches along the side of the tongue that won't wipe away.
pearl: Unlike thrush, oral hairy leukoplakia won't scrape off. In someone not known to be immunosuppressed, it's an indication for an HIV test.

title: A pale patch
context: A 35-year-old from a country where it's endemic, with a pale patch on the skin that feels numb to touch.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC
img.alt: Close-up of skin with a pale, round plaque-like patch and a smaller lesion nearby.

hints: The numbness is the key clue.
Feel for thickened nerves nearby.
why: A pale, slightly raised patch of skin, which in this story has lost sensation.
pearl: A pale patch that has lost sensation is leprosy until proven otherwise. It's curable with multidrug therapy and is not highly contagious. It still exists, including in parts of northern Australia.

title: Look at the nails
context: A 34-year-old woman with heavy periods, tiredness and breathlessness on stairs.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC
img.alt: Both hands showing flattened, spoon-shaped fingernails, most obvious on the thumbnails.

hints: Could they hold a drop of water?
Think of the commonest nutritional deficiency in the world.
why: Thin, flattened, spoon-shaped nails, most obvious on the thumbs.
pearl: Koilonychia classically means iron deficiency. Find the cause: in women think heavy periods; in men and post-menopausal women, the gut until proven otherwise.

title: Look at the eyes
context: A 29-year-old back from a holiday, with a week of nausea, dark urine and pale stools.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Thomas F. Sellers/Emory University (cropped)
img.alt: Close-up of eyes with yellow sclerae and yellowish facial skin in a patient with hepatitis A.

hints: Check the urine colour in the story again.
Bilirubin above about 50 µmol/L shows here first.
why: Yellow sclerae: bilirubin deposits in the elastin-rich white of the eye.
pearl: Carotenaemia (too many carrots) yellows the skin but spares the sclerae. Dark urine with pale stools points to a conjugated, obstructive or hepatic cause.

title: Crusty sores
context: A 9-year-old with spreading sores on the arm after scratching insect bites. Classmates have it too.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Dr Herman Miranda, Univ. of Trujillo, Peru; A. Chambers
img.alt: Crusted skin lesions on the inner surface of a forearm.

hints: The crusts are often described as honey-coloured.
Highly contagious and common in school-aged children.
why: Superficial erosions with golden-brown crusts on the forearm.
pearl: In remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, school sores (strep impetigo) are linked to rheumatic fever and kidney disease, so they matter more than they look.

title: Rings on the chest
context: A man who works with cattle, with a few slowly spreading itchy rings on his chest.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Dr Lucille K. Georg
img.alt: A man's chest with several reddened ring-shaped skin lesions.

hints: The edge is scaly and active; the centre clears.
Scrape the edge and look under the microscope.
why: Ring-shaped red lesions with a raised scaly edge and clearer centres.
pearl: Topical steroids make ringworm spread and look odd ('tinea incognito'). Treat with a topical antifungal for a week or two after it clears.

title: Tiny dots
context: A 60-year-old living alone on toast and tea, with bleeding gums, easy bruising and poor wound healing.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC
img.alt: Close-up of skin with numerous small haemorrhages centred on hair follicles.

hints: Each dot sits around a hair follicle.
Look for corkscrew hairs too.
why: Small red-brown haemorrhages centred on hair follicles.
pearl: Scurvy hasn't gone away: think of it in older people living alone, heavy drinkers and people on very restricted diets. It responds quickly to vitamin C.

title: Spots everywhere
context: A patient with fever and swollen lymph nodes, followed by a rash. All the spots look much the same.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Brian W.J. Mahy, BSc, MA, PhD, ScD, DSc
img.alt: Right arm and torso of a patient with a widespread pustular rash.

hints: The swollen lymph nodes are a key difference from smallpox.
Previously called monkeypox.
why: Firm, deep-seated pustules and crusts across the arm and trunk, mostly at the same stage.
pearl: Prominent lymphadenopathy helps tell mpox from smallpox. Since 2022 most cases have spread through close or sexual contact, sometimes with only a few genital or anal lesions. A vaccine is available.

title: A sore on the hand
context: A farmer bottle-feeding lambs this spring has a firm nodule on the hand. Otherwise well.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/Dr James H. Nakano
img.alt: Close-up of skin with two lesions, one crusted and one raised and fluid-filled.

hints: Sheep and goats carry it, especially around their lambs' mouths.
It's a parapoxvirus, and it heals on its own in about six weeks.
why: A firm, red, target-like nodule beside a fluid-filled lesion that is crusting.
pearl: Orf usually heals without treatment. Milker's nodule looks almost identical but comes from cattle. Ask everyone with a hand lump what animals they handle.

title: Look at the neck
context: A middle-aged man from a mountainous inland region, far from the sea, with a slowly growing lump.
question: What's the sign?

img.author: CDC/ Robert S. Craig (cropped)
img.alt: A man with a large anterior neck swelling from an iodine-deficiency goitre.

hints: It would move up when he swallows.
Iodised salt has made this far rarer.
why: A large, diffuse swelling of the lower front of the neck: an enlarged thyroid gland.
pearl: Iodine deficiency is still the commonest cause of goitre worldwide. A thyroid lump moves on swallowing; a thyroglossal cyst also moves when the tongue sticks out.

title: Patches of white
context: A 19-year-old with painless, flat pale patches on the trunk that burn easily in the sun. No itch, no scale.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/ Brian Hill, New Zealand
img.alt: Torso of a young man with irregular, depigmented whitish-pink patches.

hints: The patches are completely white, not just paler.
Under a Wood's lamp they glow bright white.
why: Sharply defined, completely depigmented patches with normal skin texture.
pearl: Vitiligo is autoimmune loss of melanocytes. Pityriasis versicolor is scaly and partly pale; leprosy patches are numb. Check thyroid function.

title: Up close
context: A school note went home about an itchy scalp outbreak. This is what the microscope showed on a few hairs.
question: What are you looking at?

img.author: CDC/Dr Dennis Juranek
img.alt: Close-up of three louse eggs stuck to hair shafts at different stages of development.

hints: They are glued to the hair shaft and won't slide off.
The parent insect has six legs.
why: Oval eggs cemented to hair shafts near the scalp, at different stages of development.
pearl: Nits are glued on; dandruff and hair casts slide off. Nits more than about 1 cm from the scalp are usually empty shells, so they don't prove active infestation.

title: Look at the elbow
context: A 45-year-old with thick, itchy patches on the elbows and knees for years, worse in winter.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/ Susan Lindsley
img.alt: Back of the left elbow with red, scaly psoriatic plaques.

hints: Extensor surfaces, not the creases.
Check the nails for pits.
why: Well-defined red plaques with thick silvery scale over the extensor elbow.
pearl: Psoriasis likes extensor surfaces; eczema likes flexures. Up to a third of people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis, so ask about joints.

title: Sun-exposed skin
context: A heavy drinker with diarrhoea, confusion and a rash only on the backs of the hands.
question: What's the diagnosis?

img.author: CDC/ Emory University, Dr. Thomas F. Sellers
img.alt: Back of a hand with dark, dry, peeling dermatitis on sun-exposed skin.

hints: Remember the 'three Ds' (plus a fourth).
It's a vitamin B3 deficiency.
why: Dark, dry, peeling dermatitis sharply limited to sun-exposed skin on the back of the hand.
pearl: The four Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia and death. A rash in a band around the neck is called Casal's necklace.
